## What is R?

[R](https://www.r-project.org) is a programming language designed for working with data. You can use it to import, clean, analyse, and visualise data, and to report your results, all by writing code.

A few things worth knowing:

- R is a language, not a program with menus - you tell R what to do by typing commands, which you can save, edit, and rerun.
- R is free and open source - anyone can download it, read how it works, and contribute to it.
- R was built by statisticians - it grew out of the S language and was created in the 1990s at the University of Auckland (it is now maintained by a global community).
- R is extended by packages - Researchers share tools for specialised tasks as add-on packages, from fossil range analysis to phylogenetics.

## R and RStudio

R and RStudio are two separate things, and it helps to know the differences. [R](https://www.r-project.org) is the language and engine that runs your code while [RStudio](https://posit.co/products/open-source/rstudio) is a workspace that makes R easier to use.

> *R is like as a car's engine while RStudio is the car's dashboard and controls.*

In this module, you will be typing into RStudio, but R does the work.

## Why use R?

You may already analyse data in a spreadsheet. Spreadsheets are fine for storing and eyeballing small tables, but R offers several advantages for research.

### Reproducibility

Every step of your analysis is written down. Anyone, including you in six months, can rerun your script and get the same result. With point-and-click tools, the steps live only in your memory.

### Transparency and trust

Code records exactly what you did to your data: what you removed, what you transformed, and which model you ran. Reviewers and collaborators can check it, and mistakes are easier to spot and fix.

### Scale and speed

Once you have written code for one dataset, you can run it on a hundred. Repetitive tasks that take hours by hand take seconds, and rerunning an analysis after you add new data costs nothing.

### Flexibility

R can handle almost any analysis or plot you can imagine. You are not limited to the options someone else put in a menu.

### A huge community

- There are >25,000 packages available on [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org), the main package repository
- Most methods in palaeontology, ecology, and evolution have an R implementation
- Help is easy to find, from documentation and tutorials to forums and colleagues

### It is a career skill

Familiarity with R is valued across academia, conservation, government, and industry, and the skills you build transfer to other languages (e.g. Python).

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Trade-Off

Like most skills in life, R has a learning curve. Expect to make typos, see error messages, and feel slow at first. This is normal for everyone, but the payoff comes quickly as the basics become second nature.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Exercise 1: Think about the last time you analysed or plotted data

1. Could someone else have repeated exactly what you did?
2. How long would it take you to rerun the whole analysis on a new dataset?
:::

## Basic syntax, functions, and object classes

At its simplest, R is a very powerful calculator. Type an expression into the console (or run it from a script) and R returns the result.

```{r}
#| label: basic-syntax

2 + 3
10 / 4
2^3
```

### Objects and assignment

In R, we use `<-` to store a value in an object. Once stored, you can reuse the object by name.

```{r}
#| label: object-assignment

n_species <- 25
n_species * 2
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## R is case-sensitive

`age_ma` and `Age_Ma` are different objects, so choose short, descriptive names without spaces.
:::

### Vectors

A vector is a collection of values of the same type. You can create one with `c()`.

```{r}
#| label: vectors

ages <- c(5.3, 11.6, 23.0, 33.9)
ages
```

Vectors can store more than numbers.

```{r}

#For instance, epochs within the Neogene
Neogene <- c("Pliocene","Miocene")
Neogene

#They can even hold logical (true/false) values
ages>20
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### Comments

Anything after `#` is a comment. R ignores comments, so use them to explain your code to your future self.

```{r}
#| label: comments

# Store the age of a fossil (in millions of years)
age_ma <- 23.5
```
:::

### Functions

A function is a reusable set of instructions that takes an input, does something with it, and returns a result. You have already used one `c()` when creating a vector.

To use (or "call") a function, type its name followed by parentheses. The values you put inside the parentheses are its **arguments**, which are the inputs the function works on.

```{r}
#| label: function-call

sqrt(x = 16)
```

`sqrt` is the function and `16` is the argument. As you can probably guess, `sqrt()` computes the square root of its argument. A function can take several arguments, separated by commas. You can supply them by position or by name.

Here are a couple more examples:

```{r}
#| label: function-examples

# log() computes the natural log
log(100)

# seq() generates sequences of numbers
a <- seq(1,10)
a <- seq(from=1, to=10) #another way to specify the arguments, see ?seq
a <- 1:10 #you can also generate a sequence using a colon
a

# other useful mathematical and statistical operations
mean(a)
median(a)
sd(a)
min(a)
max(a)
sum(a)
quantile(a)
```

### Object classes

Every object has a class, which tells R how to treat it. Check it with `class()`.

```{r}
#| label: classes

# Numeric
class(23.5)
# Integer
class(5L)
# Character
class("Acropora")
# Logical
class(TRUE)
# Factor
class(factor(c("reef-building", "non-reef-building")))
```

  | Class       | Example      | Used for                     |
  | :---------- | :----------- | :--------------------------- |
  | `numeric`   | `23.5`       | Measurements, ages           |
  | `integer`   | `5L`         | Counts                       |
  | `character` | `"Acropora"` | Names, labels                |
  | `logical`   | `TRUE`       | Yes/no conditions            |
  | `factor`    | `"reef"`     | Categories with fixed levels |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Mixing classes

Mixing classes in one vector forces R to convert everything to the most flexible class.

```{r}
#| label: mixing-classes

# Everything becomes character
class(c(1, "two", TRUE))
```
:::

### Data frames and lists

A **data frame** is a table where each column is a vector and all columns have the same length. A **list** can hold objects of different types and sizes.

```{r}
#| label: dataframe

corals <- data.frame(
  genus = c("Acropora", "Porites", "Pocillopora", "Caryophyllia", "Balanophyllia"),
  age_ka = c(23.0, 15.9, 11.6, 5.3, 2.6),
  n_specimens  = c(12L, 30L, 8L, 5L, 3L)
)
corals
class(corals)
```

You can use `$` and `[[ ]]` to extract a whole column as a **vector**.

```{r}
#| label: dataframe-access

corals$genus
corals[["genus"]]
corals[[1]]
```

Single square brackets `[ ]` also select columns, but what you get back depends on how you use them. With one index, you get a **data frame**. With a comma, you are using `[rows, columns]`, and leaving the rows blank returns every row.

```{r}
#| label: dataframe-single-brackets

corals["genus"]
corals[1]
corals[, "genus"]
corals[, 1]
corals[c("genus", "age_ka")]
```

::: {.callout-caution}
## Exercise 2: Select the second row and "genus" column

Use single square brackets `[rows, columns]` with the `corals` data frame.

1. Select the value in the second row of the `genus` column, first by column name and then by column position.
2. Select the whole second row (all columns).
3. Select the first three rows of the `genus` and `age_ka` columns.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise-2-solution

# 1. Second row, genus column
corals[2, "genus"]
corals[2, 2 - 1]

# 2. Whole second row
corals[2, ]

# 3. First three rows, two columns
corals[1:3, c("genus", "age_ka")]
```
:::

Create a list with `list()`. Each element can be a different class and length, and can even be a whole data frame.

```{r}
#| label: list

coral_specimens <- list(
  institution = "Natural History Museum",
  collection = "Fossil Cnidaria",
  genera = corals$genera,
  data = corals
)
coral_specimens
class(coral_specimens)
length(coral_specimens)
```

Use `$` or double square brackets `[[ ]]` to extract an element by name or position.

```{r}
#| label: list-access

coral_specimens$site
coral_specimens[["genera"]]
coral_specimens[[4]]
coral_specimens$data$age_ka
```

Use `str()` for a compact overview of any list.

```{r}
#| label: list-str

str(coral_specimens)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
A data frame is really just a list in which every element is a vector of the same length. Check with `is.list(corals)`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Exercise 3: Add a new element

Add a new element called `observer` to `coral_specimens`, holding your name. Then extract the `genus` column of the data frame stored inside the list.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: list-answer

coral_specimens$observer <- "Your name"
coral_specimens$data$genus
```
:::

### Missing values

R represents missing data as `NA`. Most summary functions return `NA` if any value is missing, unless you tell them otherwise.

```{r}
#| label: missing-values
#| 
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
mean(x)
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Import and view datasets

### R built-in datasets

R comes with many built-in example datasets. You can list them with `data()`:

```{r}
#| label: list-data

data()
```

And also load them by name:

```{r}
#| label: interval-data

data(iris)
head(iris)
```

### Read and write datasets

In most cases, you are going to want to use your own dataset. These can come in various formats, but one of the most common formats is a comma-separated values (`.csv`) file. In R, we can load this file using `read.csv()`:

```{r}
#| label: read-data
#| eval: true

reefs <- read.csv("reefs.csv")
```

::: {.callout-note}
`read.csv()` looks for files relative to your **working directory**. If you are working in an RStudio Project (more on this later), this is the project folder. Check it with `getwd()`.
:::

Similarly, we can also save files via R. Here, we pass the object we want to save (`reefs`) and the file name to write to:

```{r}
#| label: write-data
#| eval: false

write.csv(reefs, "reefs_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
If a file with the same name already exists, R will overwrite it without warning. Use a new file name (e.g. `reefs_clean.csv`) to avoid replacing your original data.
:::

Similar functions exist for other file formats. The table below lists some of the most common ones using base R. However, many other options exist when extending base R with packages (e.g. `.xlsx`, `.xls` formats).

  | File type                                      | Read                  | Write                     |
  | :--------------------------                    | :-------------------- | :--------------------     |
  | Comma-separated (`.csv`)                       | `read.csv()`          | `write.csv()`             |
  | Semicolon-separated (`.csv`, common in Europe) | `read.csv2()`         | `write.csv2()`            |
  | Tab-separated (`.tsv`, `.txt`)                 | `read.delim()`        | `write.table(sep = "\t")` |
  | Any delimited text file                        | `read.table()`        | `write.table()`           |
  | R data file (`.rds`)                           | `readRDS()`           | `saveRDS()`               |
  | R workspace (`.RData`, `.rda`)                 | `load()`              | `save()`                  |

### Inspect structure and summaries

Always inspect your data straight after importing it.

```{r}
head(reefs)
tail(reefs)
dim(reefs)
names(reefs)
str(reefs)
summary(reefs)
```

In RStudio, `View(reefs)` opens the data in a spreadsheet-style viewer.

::: {.callout-caution}
## Exercise 3: Practise syntax with a dataset

Load the built-in `iris` dataset and answer the following using the functions above.

1. How many rows and columns does it have?
2. What are the column names, and what class is each column?
3. What is the mean `Sepal.Length`?
4. Does the dataset contain any missing values?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise 3: Solution

**1. How many rows and columns does it have?**

```{r}
#| label: iris-dim

dim(iris)
nrow(iris)
ncol(iris)
```

The dataset has `r nrow(iris)` rows and `r ncol(iris)` columns.

**2. What are the column names, and what class is each column?**

```{r}
#| label: iris-names-class
#| output-fold: true
#| output-summary: "Output"

names(iris)
str(iris)
```

`str(iris)` returns the column names, classes and example values in one go.

**3. What is the mean `Sepal.Length`?**

```{r}
#| label: iris-mean

mean(iris$Sepal.Length)
```

**4. Does the dataset contain any missing values?**

```{r}
#| label: iris-na

anyNA(iris)
sum(is.na(iris))
colSums(is.na(iris))
```

No. `anyNA()` returns `FALSE` and the total number of `NA` values is 0.
:::

### Wrangle data

When working with datasets, you'll often need to wrangle the data to prepare them for analysis. For instance, you might want to add a column.

```{r}
#| label: reef-column

reefs$is_coral <- reefs$biota_main=="Corals"
```

Or you might want to subset your data. One option is to use the `subset()` function. For example, let's look at the Neogene and Quaternary reefs.

```{r}
#| label: reef-subset-age

reefs_neogene <- subset(reefs,system=="Neogene")
reefs_quaternary <- subset(reefs,system=="Quaternary")
reefs_neo_quat <- subset(reefs,system=="Neogene" | system=="Quaternary")
```

You can also use brackets for indexing as introduced above. Let's look at just the coral reefs.

```{r}
#| label: reef-subset-coral

reefs_coral <- reefs[reefs$biota_main=="Corals",]
```

Maybe you're interested in a certain modern-day latitudinal range. *Consider: why might this approach be problematic when analyzing fossil reefs?*

```{r}
#| label: reef-subset-lat

reefs_lat <- reefs[reefs$lat < 23.5 & reefs$lat > -23.5,] #tropics
```

We could also subset this data frame further to just pull out the Holocene occurrences.

```{r}
#| label: reef-subset-lat-age

reefs_lat[which(reefs_lat$series=="Holocene"),]
```

You might want to sort your data. Note that you can also do this when directly viewing the dataset in RStudio, i.e. with `View()`.

```{r}
#| label: reef-sort
#| output: false

#Putting them into descending order by citation year
reefs[order(reefs$year, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

You might want to combine datasets. `rbind()` combines rows. `cbind()` combines columns. `merge()` will join dataframes. Let's recombine two of our subsets from above using rbind() as an example.

```{r}
#| label: reef-combine

reefs_combined <- rbind(reefs_neogene,reefs_quaternary)
```

And you may want to tabulate the data. Let's look at how much data there are across the different intervals in the full reef dataset.

```{r}
#| label: reef-tabulate

table(reefs$system)
```

All of these operations can be done in base R as well as using tidyverse syntax. For additional practice manipulating data frames using `dplyr`, see the tidyverse module. For additional practice cleaning and preparing data for analysis, see the *Data cleaning* and *Data exploration* modules.

### Plot variables

Finally, you may want to plot your data. We'll cover a basic example here in base R. For a more in-depth treatment of plotting, see the *ggplot2* and *Data visualisation* modules.

Let's first make a histogram of the latitudes present in the dataset.

```{r}
#| label: plotting-hist

hist(reefs$lat,breaks=10)

# Layering the reef occurrences on top of the full dataset...Does anything look odd to you?
hist(reefs$lat,breaks=10)
hist(reefs_coral$lat,col="coral",add=TRUE)
```

Let's also practice making a scatterplot. Here, I'm going to generate a toy dataset using `rnorm()`so you can see how to do that.

```{r}
#| label: plotting-scatter

#rnorm() randomly generates data following a normal distribution
x <- rnorm(20,mean=2,sd=1)
y <- rnorm(20,mean=5,sd=2)

#plot
plot(y~x,type="p",cex=1.5,pch=21,col="black",bg="cornflowerblue",xlab="x",ylab="y")
```

::: {.callout-caution}
## Exercise 4: Practise wrangling and plotting data

Now it's your turn. Use the `iris` dataset that you've already loaded to do the following:

1. Subset the data to look at just the *setosa* and *versicolor* species.
2. Plot the relationship between petal length and width. Color the points by species.
3. Add a column that calculates the ratio of petal length to width.
4. Make a boxplot comparing the petal ratios between the two species. Plot the mean ratio values as points on top of the boxplot. How do the petal dimensions differ between the two species?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise 4: Solution

**1. Subset the data to look at just the *setosa* and *versicolor* species.**

```{r}
#| label: iris-subset

iris_subset <- subset(iris, Species=="setosa" | Species=="versicolor")
```

**2. Plot the relationship between petal length and width. Color the points by species.**

```{r}
#| label: iris-scatterplot

# Hint: Drop levels prior to plotting; otherwise, you'll find a phantom species in your legend! 
iris_subset$Species <- droplevels(iris_subset$Species)
levels(iris_subset$Species)

# Custom colors
cols <- c("setosa" = "steelblue", "versicolor" = "orange")

# Plot width~length
plot(iris_subset$Petal.Width~iris_subset$Petal.Length,
     col = cols[iris$Species],
     pch = 19,
     xlab = "Petal length (cm)",
     ylab = "Petal width (cm)",
     main = "Iris petal dimensions")

legend("topleft",
       legend = levels(iris_subset$Species),
       col = cols[levels(iris_subset$Species)],
       pch = 19)
```

**3. Add a column that calculates the ratio of petal length to width.**

```{r}
#| label: iris-new-col

# Add a column for the ratio of Petal.Length/Petal.Width
iris_subset$Petal.Ratio <- iris_subset$Petal.Length/iris_subset$Petal.Width
```

**4. Make a boxplot comparing the petal ratios between the two species. Plot the mean ratio values as points on top of the boxplot. How do the petal dimensions differ between the two species?**

```{r}
#| label: iris-boxplot

# Plot
boxplot(Petal.Ratio ~ Species, data = iris_subset,
        col = cols[levels(iris_subset$Species)],
        xlab = "Species",
        ylab = "Petal length / width ratio",
        main = "Petal ratio by species")

# Calculate mean ratio for each species
setosa_mean <- mean(iris_subset$Petal.Ratio[iris_subset$Species=="setosa"])
versicolor_mean <- mean(iris_subset$Petal.Ratio[iris_subset$Species=="versicolor"])

# Add means to the plot
mean_ratio <- c(setosa_mean,versicolor_mean)
points(1:2, mean_ratio, pch = 18, cex = 2, col = "black")
```

We see clear separation between the two species in terms of their petal dimensions. *versicolor* has larger petals than *setosa*. The petal shape also differs between species: *versicolor* petals have a lower aspect ratio than *setosa*, meaning that they are rounder.
:::

## More advanced operations

### If/else statements

If/else statements allow you to make conditional statements: R will do something only under certain conditions.

```{r}
#| label: if-else

#run with one value
x <- 4
if(x>3) print ("x is greater than 3") else print ("oh no!")

#run with another value to show how the outcome changes
x <- 2
if(x>3) print ("x is greater than 3") else print ("oh no!")

#ifelse() for simple logical tests
y <- c(0,1,10,12,50,0)
z <- ifelse(y>0,1,0)
z
```

### Loops

Loops are useful for repeated operations.

```{r}
#| label: loops

for (i in iris$Sepal.Length[1:5]){ #Just pulling the first 5 sepal length values as an example
  Sepal.Length.mm <- i * 10 #converts from cm to mm
  print(Sepal.Length.mm) #prints output
}
```

### Apply

There's another way to do this using apply functions. 

```{r}
#| label: sapply

sapply(iris$Sepal.Length[1:5], function(x) x * 10) #using sapply() since we're dealing with a vector
```

Here's another example using `apply()` to find the minimum sepal length and width in the `iris` dataset.

```{r}
#| label: apply

apply(iris[,1:2], 2, min)
```

## Writing functions

Today, we'll just dip our toes into the world of writing your own functions. To dive in deeper, check out the *Writing functions* module.

Let's write a basic function together to understand its structure.

Example: Palaeoverse team members Lewis and Erin are both avid runners but are having trouble comparing how far they ran. Let's help them convert between miles and kilometers.
```{r}
#| label: function-writing

# Simple version that converts from miles to kilometers
mi_to_km <- function(mi){ # specify name and arguments
  km <- mi*1.609344 # body, which performs the operation
  return(km) # what gets returned
}

# Test it out
mi_to_km(6)


# Let's make this even more interchangeable using an if/else statement
convert_distance <- function(distance, units = c("mi", "km")) {
  units <- match.arg(units) #controls the input

  if (units == "mi") {
    distance * 1.609344   # miles to km
  } else {
    distance / 1.609344   # km to miles
  }
}

# Test it out
convert_distance(18,"km")
```

::: {.callout-caution}
## Exercise 5: Practise writing a function

Practise writing a function of your own! You can either be creative or attempt the following example:

1. Write a function that can place values (e.g., size measurements) into three groups (small, medium, large) based on user-specified threshold values. *Hint: ifelse() may come in handy*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise 5: Solution

**1. Write a function that can place values (e.g., size measurements) into three groups (small, medium, large) based on user-specified threshold values.**

```{r}
#| label: function-solution
 
classify_size <- function(size, small = 10, large = 30) { #providing some defaults
  ifelse(size < small, "small",
         ifelse(size < large, "medium", "large")) 
}

# Test it out
classify_size(10)
classify_size(25)
classify_size(32)
```
:::

## Libraries

Everything we've done so far in this tutorial has relied on functions that are built into base R. However, there's a big world of functions out there that can do everything from tidying up data to making beautiful plots to running statistical and other discipline-specific analyses. The possibilities are nearly endless (and if you do hit a hall, you can even make your own package!).

To tap into this world, you install packages. You can either do this in the Output panel under the Packages tab (click "Install" and then type and select the package name). You can also script the installation, which can be helpful if you need to install several packages. Note that you only need to install a package once; after that, it lives in your library. 

```{r}
#| label: install-packages
#| eval: false

install.packages("palaeoverse")
```

This gives you access to the tens of thousands of packages available on CRAN. But wait...there's more. To download a package directly from GitHub (i.e., development versions or packages that are not available on CRAN), you can use the `devtools` package.

```{r}
#| label: install-devtools
#| eval: false

install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("palaeoverse/palaeoverse")
```

Prior to using any of the functions in a package, you'll need to load it. Then you're good to go!
```{r}
#| label: load-packages

library(palaeoverse)
```

To access the documentation, type `?` and the package name.
```{r}
#| label: documentation

?palaeoverse
```

Are you feeling powerful yet?
